AI Compass

History of AI: a timeline from 1950 to today

From a single question in 1950 to the AI in your pocket today.

Early ideas (1950 – 1972)

Big questions, first programs and huge hopes.

🤔 1950: Alan Turing asks: “Can machines think?”

In his paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, the British mathematician Alan Turing proposed the “imitation game”: a judge chats by typed messages with a person and with a machine. If the judge can't tell which is which, perhaps the machine should count as intelligent.

Why it matters. It turned a big philosophical question into a test you could actually run, known today as the Turing test.

Turing testLesson 1: What is AI?

🏫 1956: The Dartmouth workshop gives AI its name

In the summer of 1956, scientists met at Dartmouth College in the USA for a workshop. The plan for it, written by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester, used a new name for the field: “artificial intelligence”.

Why it matters. AI became a field of research with its own name — and with very big hopes about how quickly it would succeed.

Artificial intelligence (AI)Lesson 1: What is AI?

🔗 1958: The perceptron: a machine that learns

Psychologist Frank Rosenblatt introduced the perceptron, one of the first artificial neural networks. It learned to recognise simple patterns by adjusting its weights after every mistake. A later machine version, the Mark I Perceptron, looked at pictures through a “camera” of 400 light sensors.

Why it matters. It showed that a machine could learn from examples instead of following fixed rules, the idea behind today's neural networks.

Artificial neuronNeural networkLesson 3: Neural Networks

🏁 1959: Machine learning gets its name

At IBM, Arthur Samuel wrote a program that played checkers (draughts) and got better by playing game after game against a copy of itself. In a 1959 paper he called this “machine learning”, and he reported that the program had learned to play better than he did.

Why it matters. It gave the field a name and an idea that still drives AI: instead of programming every move, let the computer learn from experience.

Machine learning (ML)TrainingLesson 2: Machine Learning

💬 1966: ELIZA, one of the first chatbots

At MIT, Joseph Weizenbaum created ELIZA, a program that chatted like a therapist using simple rules: it spotted key words in what you typed and turned your own words back into questions.

Why it matters. Many people felt that ELIZA understood them although it understood nothing, and this “ELIZA effect” is worth remembering when you talk to chatbots today.

ChatbotNatural language processing (NLP)Lesson 4: Generative AI & Chatbots

🤖 1966–72: Shakey, a robot that plans its own moves

At the Stanford Research Institute (SRI) in California, a team built Shakey, a robot on wheels with a TV camera. Given a task such as pushing a box into another room, it looked around, made a plan and carried it out step by step. It got its name because it shook as it moved.

Why it matters. Methods invented for Shakey, such as the A* route-finding search, are still used in robots and video games today.

RobotAgent

Ups & downs (1970s – 2011)

Hype and funding cuts, famous wins, and the quiet work that prepared a comeback.

❄️ 1970s–80s: The “AI winters”

Early AI promised too much, too soon, and computers were still slow and expensive. When the results disappointed, money for research dried up: in Britain, a 1973 report for the government judged that AI had not kept its promises. A second “winter” came in the late 1980s, when the boom in expert systems ended.

Why it matters. It is a lesson about hype: big promises that aren't kept can freeze progress for years.

🩺 1980s: Expert systems: knowledge as rules

Expert systems stored the know-how of human specialists as hundreds or thousands of “if … then …” rules. MYCIN, built at Stanford University in the 1970s, used such rules to suggest treatments for blood infections. In the 1980s, expert systems became big business.

Why it matters. They brought AI into companies, but hand-written rules were costly to keep up to date and broke on unusual cases, one reason why AI later turned to learning from data.

Expert systemAlgorithmLesson 1: What is AI?

🔁 1986: Neural networks learn from their mistakes

David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams showed how a neural network with several layers can learn. After each answer, a method called backpropagation works out how much every connection added to the error and adjusts it a little. The idea was older, but their 1986 paper made it famous.

Why it matters. Backpropagation is still how almost every neural network is trained today.

BackpropagationNeural networkGradient descentLoss functionLesson 3: Neural Networks

✍️ 1989: A neural network learns to read handwriting

At Bell Labs in the USA, Yann LeCun and his colleagues trained a convolutional neural network to read handwritten digits, such as ZIP codes (postcodes) on letters. Nobody wrote rules for it: it learned from thousands of examples which shapes make a 3 or a 7. In the 1990s, banks used later versions (LeNet) to read handwritten numbers on cheques.

Why it matters. It proved that neural networks could do a real everyday job, and its design is the ancestor of the networks that recognise faces and objects in photos today.

Convolutional neural network (CNN)Computer visionLesson 7: How Computers See

♟️ 1997: Deep Blue beats the world chess champion

IBM's computer Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in a six-game match, 3½–2½. It didn't learn the way modern AI does: special chess chips let it check about 200 million positions every second.

Why it matters. For the first time, a computer beat the reigning world champion in a match under tournament conditions, showing what raw computing power could do.

AlgorithmLesson 1: What is AI?

🚗 2005: A robot car crosses the desert on its own

In a race organised by DARPA, a research agency of the US Department of Defense, robot cars had to drive themselves across the desert with nobody inside. In 2004, none of them reached the finish. In 2005, five did, and Stanley from Stanford University won: it drove the 212-kilometre course faster than all the others.

Why it matters. It started the race to build self-driving cars, and by 2025 taxis with no driver were carrying passengers in several cities.

RobotComputer visionLesson 5: AI in Everyday Life

🏷️ 2009: ImageNet: millions of labelled photos

Fei-Fei Li and her team presented ImageNet, a huge collection of photos, each labelled by people working online with what it shows. It grew to more than 14 million images in over 20,000 categories, from strawberries to sports cars. From 2010, a yearly contest used it to find out which program recognised pictures best.

Why it matters. It showed how much good data AI needs to learn, and its contest became the stage where deep learning made its breakthrough in 2012.

DatasetComputer visionLesson 2: Machine Learning

🎙️ 2011: Watson wins Jeopardy!, and Siri arrives

IBM's Watson beat two of the best champions of the TV quiz show Jeopardy!, answering tricky questions asked in everyday English. In the same year, Apple built the voice assistant Siri into the iPhone 4S. Siri wasn't the first voice assistant, but it put one into millions of pockets.

Why it matters. Computers were getting much better at understanding everyday language, and AI started moving into people's pockets.

Natural language processing (NLP)Lesson 5: AI in Everyday Life

Deep learning (2012 – 2020)

Neural networks, big data and fast chips change everything.

🖼️ 2012: AlexNet starts the deep-learning boom

A deep neural network called AlexNet, built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, won the ImageNet image-recognition contest by a huge margin. Allowed five guesses per photo, it missed the right answer only about 15% of the time, against 26% for the next best entry. It was trained on graphics cards (GPUs) — chips first made for video games.

Why it matters. It proved that big neural networks, lots of data and fast chips really work together, and within a few years deep learning was everywhere: in photos, speech and translation.

Deep learningConvolutional neural network (CNN)Computer visionLesson 7: How Computers See

🔢 2013: word2vec turns words into numbers

A team at Google led by Tomas Mikolov released word2vec, a method that turns every word into a list of numbers, learned from billions of words of text. Words used in similar ways get similar numbers, and you can even do maths with meaning: “king” − “man” + “woman” lands close to “queen”.

Why it matters. Numbers that capture the meaning of words, called embeddings, became a basic building block of today's language models.

EmbeddingNatural language processing (NLP)Lesson 9: How Chatbots Write

🎨 2014: GANs: AI learns to create images

Ian Goodfellow and his colleagues invented generative adversarial networks (GANs). Two neural networks compete like a forger and a detective: one makes fake images, the other tries to spot the fakes, and both keep getting better.

Why it matters. Computers began to create realistic new pictures, which paved the way for today's generative AI — and also for deepfakes.

Generative adversarial network (GAN)Generative AIDeepfakeLesson 10: Creative AI

⚫ 2016: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol at Go

DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's best Go players, 4–1 in Seoul. Go has more possible board positions than there are atoms in the observable universe, so simply checking every move could never work.

Why it matters. Learning first from human games and then by playing against itself (reinforcement learning), AlphaGo found new ideas, like its famous “Move 37”, that surprised even top players.

Reinforcement learningRewardLesson 8: Learning by Trial and Error

⚡ 2017: The Transformer: “Attention Is All You Need”

Researchers at Google published a paper that introduced the Transformer, a new neural network design. It uses “attention” to look at all the words of a text at once and work out how they relate to each other.

Why it matters. Transformers became the basis of almost every modern language model: the “T” in GPT stands for Transformer.

TransformerAttentionLesson 9: How Chatbots Write

⚖️ 2018: Gender Shades: AI that isn't equally accurate for everyone

Researchers Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial AI systems that guess a person's gender from a photo. For lighter-skinned men they were wrong at most 0.8% of the time, but for darker-skinned women up to 34.7% of the time. The face collections used to test such systems showed mostly lighter-skinned people, so the problem had gone unnoticed.

Why it matters. It showed why AI must be tested on different groups of people, not just on average, and the companies soon improved their systems.

BiasDatasetLesson 11: Can You Trust AI?

📝 2020: GPT-3: a giant language model

OpenAI introduced GPT-3, a language model with 175 billion parameters, trained to predict the next word on huge amounts of text from the internet and books. With no extra training it could write stories, answer questions, translate or write simple code, just from a few examples in the prompt.

Why it matters. It showed that making language models much bigger made them surprisingly capable, which led to ChatGPT two years later.

Large language model (LLM)Parameters (weights)Next-token predictionLesson 9: How Chatbots Write

🧬 2020: AlphaFold 2: a breakthrough in biology

At the CASP14 science competition, DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted the 3D shapes of proteins from their building blocks, often almost as accurately as lab experiments. Scientists had been working on this problem for about 50 years.

Why it matters. A protein's shape helps explain how it works and how diseases might be treated, and AlphaFold's free database now holds predicted shapes for over 200 million proteins.

Deep learning

Generative AI (2022 – today)

AI that writes, draws and talks — now in everyone's hands.

🖌️ 2022: Type a sentence, get a picture

Image generators such as DALL·E 2 and Stable Diffusion turned short descriptions into detailed pictures. They are diffusion models: they start from random noise and remove it step by step until an image that matches the words appears. Stable Diffusion was released openly, so anyone could run it on a good home computer.

Why it matters. Making pictures became as easy as typing, which raised big questions about artists' work used for training, about copyright and about fake photos.

Diffusion modelGenerative AIPromptLesson 10: Creative AI

🚀 2022: ChatGPT goes public

On 30 November 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, a chatbot built on a large language model and trained with feedback from people to be helpful. According to widely reported estimates, it reached about 100 million users in roughly two months — one of the fastest-growing apps ever.

Why it matters. Suddenly anyone could talk to AI in plain language, and generative AI became an everyday topic at school, at work and at home.

ChatbotLarge language model (LLM)Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)Lesson 4: Generative AI & Chatbots

📸 2023: Chatbots learn to see: multimodal AI

In March 2023, OpenAI released GPT-4, a model that could understand pictures as well as text, for example to describe what is in a photo (in ChatGPT, this arrived that autumn). Other companies released their own large models, such as Anthropic's Claude and Google's Gemini. Models that handle several kinds of data, like text, images and sound, are called multimodal.

Why it matters. AI assistants could now help with what you see, not only with what you type — but they still make mistakes, so their answers need checking.

Multimodal AILarge language model (LLM)HallucinationLesson 9: How Chatbots Write

📜 2024: The EU adopts the first broad law on AI

The European Union adopted the AI Act, the first broad law on artificial intelligence. It sorts AI by risk: a few uses are banned, such as scoring people for their behaviour; high-risk uses, like AI that helps decide who gets a job or a loan, must meet strict rules; and people must be told when they are talking to a chatbot.

Why it matters. For the first time, a large group of countries set binding rules for AI, which apply step by step over several years.

EU AI ActLesson 11: Can You Trust AI?

🏅 2024: Nobel Prizes for AI pioneers

The Nobel Prize in Physics went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for discoveries that made machine learning with neural networks possible. The Chemistry prize went to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for AlphaFold, together with David Baker for designing new proteins with computers.

Why it matters. Science's most famous awards recognised AI both as a field of discovery and as a powerful tool for other sciences.

Neural networkLesson 3: Neural Networks

🧠 2024–25: AI that reasons step by step, and agents that act

In September 2024, OpenAI released a preview of o1, one of the first “reasoning” models: it was trained to work through a problem step by step before answering, which made it much better at maths and coding. Others, such as DeepSeek-R1, soon followed. AI agents also appeared that can use tools, search the web or click through websites to carry out tasks with many steps.

Why it matters. AI began to move from answering questions to doing tasks, but it still makes mistakes, so people need to check its work and decide what it is allowed to do.

Reasoning modelAgentLarge language model (LLM)Lesson 12: Your AI Toolkit

📱 Today: AI in your pocket, your classroom and the lab

AI now helps to translate languages, edit photos, recommend videos, support doctors and speed up science. Many students use AI chatbots to learn — and the open questions matter as much as the technology.

Why it matters. Keeping AI fair, safe and honest, and deciding how it should change school and work, is up to people — including you.
